title: The cave of Hira
hook: near forty, he climbs to a small cave on a mountain above Mecca to think and pray alone

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Black Stone on a cloak, and every clan lifting together. Your line was everyone takes a corner. Did you find a cloak for your standoff? Day eighty-five.

He has a good life now. A loving wife, children, a solid business, a name everyone trusts. Tradition says he's nearing forty. And something in him keeps pulling him out of town. Outside Mecca there's a steep, rocky mountain. Near the top, tucked between boulders, is a cave. Tiny. Room for a person to sit, maybe to lie down, not much more. And that's where he starts going. Alone. Carrying food and water up the mountain, and staying for days and nights at a time. Not to escape his family; he keeps coming back to them. But to be somewhere quiet enough to think.
screen: `A GOOD LIFE, NEARING FORTY.` → `A STEEP MOUNTAIN, A TINY CAVE.` → `DAYS AND NIGHTS, ALONE.`

segments.voice: The cave is called Hira. The mountain is known today as Jabal an-Nur, the Mountain of Light. The account comes down in a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aishah. She says that before revelation came, he began to have dreams that came true, clear as the break of dawn. And then, in her words as they've come down, solitude was made dear to him. He would go to the cave of Hira and worship there for many nights, then come back to Khadijah for more provisions, and go again. The hadith's word for what he did there is tahannuth, and it explains the word itself: worship, night after night, a kind of spiritual retreat. What exactly he prayed, and how, the sources don't say. They tell us where, and for how long, and that he kept going back. Ibn Ishaq adds that he spent a month there every year, and that the month was Ramadan, and that he fed the poor who came to him. Remember the city he was pulling away from: the valley of idols and caravans from day seventy-eight. Up there, none of it. Wind, rock, stars, and the city small below. People still climb to Hira today. It's a hard climb, rough steps cut into the mountain, and at the top a narrow gap in the rocks. It isn't part of any required ritual. People go because he went. And because everything that comes next in his life, and in the life of Islam, starts in that small, quiet place.
screen: `JABAL AN-NUR, THE MOUNTAIN OF LIGHT.` · `SOLITUDE WAS MADE DEAR TO HIM.` · `TAHANNUTH: DAYS OF DEVOTION.` · `THE CITY SMALL BELOW.` · then, large: `GO UP TO THE QUIET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit somewhere quiet for two minutes. If you can, move. Another room, a stairwell, a parked car, the far corner of a park. Go a little higher or a little further away, if only a few steps. Then sit. Let the noise of the day get small below you, the way Mecca did from the mountain. You don't need to think of anything holy. Just be where nobody needs you for a moment. If you pray, you can simply sit with Allah, without asking for anything. The bell holds the time.
Hira, the cave on the Mountain of Light above Mecca, where he went to be alone and pray, night after night.
Your line: go up to the quiet. Today, find one pocket of time and one place where nobody needs you, and use it for nothing but quiet. Tomorrow, the night everything changes. Day eighty-five.

howItsDone: Some Muslims keep a spiritual retreat, i'tikaf, staying in the mosque in the last ten nights of Ramadan; some pilgrims to Mecca climb Jabal an-Nur to see the cave of Hira, though it is not part of the rites.

original.note: Arabic: Hira, the cave on Jabal an-Nur.

trapdoor: what you thought: he went to a cave and an angel appeared.
what it means: for a long time before anything happened, he kept climbing to a small cave to pray alone, and came back to his family.
what a scholar hears: tahannuth is glossed in the hadith itself as worship for many nights; and 'Aishah's report opens with true dreams 'like the break of dawn', falaq as-subh.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3 (true dreams; solitude made dear; tahannuth in Hira)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (a month each year in Hira, in Ramadan; feeding the poor)
sources.work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq, via Ibn Hisham)

notes: No Qur'an quotation today; the teach paraphrases 'Aishah's report in Bukhari 3. The phrase 'solitude was made dear to him' is a paraphrase in common use; confirm it isn't copied from a protected translation.
'A few miles from Mecca': Jabal an-Nur is about 2–3 miles from the Masjid al-Haram. Confirm.
Month of Ramadan and feeding the poor at Hira: from Ibn Ishaq; confirm.
'The sources don't say' how he worshiped: scholars differ (some say according to the religion of Ibrahim, some reflection). Confirm this phrasing.

Editor review 2026-10-01: cut 'the oldest account' (Ibn Ishaq is earlier than Bukhari) and the etymology 'turning away from wrongdoing' for tahannuth (the hadith glosses it only as worship); age now 'tradition says'; distance cut; softened the harsh picture of Mecca to a back-reference.
